reconcile.connective: Defenders hold that "Jabin" was a dynastic title and that Canaanites rebuilt the burned Hazor, so Judges 4 names a later king of the same name, not the one Joshua slew.

discrepancy.connective: J. Alberto Soggin argues the originally independent Deborah-Sisera tradition was secondarily fused with Joshua 11, so the "second Jabin of Hazor" is an editorial conflation of one event, not a real later king.

skeptic.name: J. Alberto Soggin
skeptic.attribution: J. Alberto Soggin (d. 2010), Judges: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (1981)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It is probable that Jabin was the common name of all the kings of Hazor. That king, by whom the Israelites were kept in a state of slavery for twenty years, and who was defeated by Deborah and Barak, was called by this name … it is likely that the Canaanites rebuilt it, and restored the ancient government, as we find a powerful king there about one hundred and thirty years after the death of Joshua, Jdg 4:1.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the tension: dynastic-name theory plus a rebuilt Hazor yields a later, different Jabin in Judges 4. Ellipsis joins two non-adjacent on-tension sentences in the same note, preserving sense.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Joshua 11:1
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage directly, arguing Jabin was a common (dynastic) name of the kings of Hazor and that Canaanites rebuilt the burned city, so the Judges 4 Jabin is a later king of the same name.
